t: The Vikings were Scandinavian raiders, traders and settlers whose voyages between the 790s and the 1060s reached from Newfoundland to the Caspian Sea and from the Arctic to the Mediterranean.
Their raids fell hardest on monasteries and towns in Britain, Ireland and Francia, but they also founded Dublin, settled Iceland and Normandy, ruled much of England and gave a dynasty to the Rus’.
At home the age saw trading towns, the first kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden and conversion to Christianity, after which royal conquest took the place of free-roving raids.
dyk: Wood cut with metal blades at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland has been dated to the year 1021 by a spike in radiocarbon that a solar storm of 993 left in tree rings: the earliest exact year known for Europeans in the Americas.
ev: Raiders plunder the monastery of Lindisfarne, the attack that usually marks the start of the Viking Age
Rus’ ships attack Constantinople; by tradition Rurik begins to rule at Novgorod two years later
The Great Heathen Army lands in England; Alfred the Great defeats it at Edington in 878
Norse settlers take land in Iceland and found the Althing, its general assembly, about 930
Rollo receives lands around Rouen from Charles the Simple, the beginning of Normandy (traditional date)
Erik the Red leads settlers from Iceland to Greenland
Leif Erikson sails to Vinland; Norse visitors cut wood at L’Anse aux Meadows in 1021
Harald Hardrada of Norway is killed at Stamford Bridge, weeks before the Battle of Hastings

f.homeland: Scandinavia, in present-day Denmark, Norway and Sweden; settlements in the British Isles, Normandy, the Faroes, Iceland and Greenland and along the rivers of present-day Russia and Ukraine
f.period: c. 793–1066, from the raid on Lindisfarne to the death of Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge; raiding at its height in the 9th century, kingdoms and conversion in the 10th and 11th
f.known: Longships; raids and tribute; the settlement of Iceland and Greenland and the voyages to Vinland; trading towns and silver hoards; runestones and sagas
f.sources: The chronicles of their victims and neighbours (the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the Annals of St Bertin, the Annals of Ulster, the Primary Chronicle, Arabic writers such as Ibn Fadlan); runic inscriptions; Icelandic sagas written down from the 13th century; excavated sites such as Hedeby, Birka, York and L’Anse aux Meadows; the Oseberg and Gokstad ships
